Each piece has four dichotomous attributes — color, height, shape, and consistency — so each piece is either black or white, tall or short, square or round, and hollow or solid. The object is to place the fourth piece in a row in which all four pieces have at least one attribute in common. The twist is that your opponent gets to choose the piece you place on the board each turn. Number of players: 2 Game duration: 4 mn Complexity: 1 / 5 Play Quarto and 1414 other games online. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Components 2 Game Play 3 Game End 4 Advanced variant Components Board with a 4×4 grid. 16 pieces with four characteristics each: Light or dark; Tall or short; Circular or square; and Solid or hollow. Each possible combination of characteristics appears exactly once. e.g. light & tall & circular & solid. e.g. dark & short & square & hollow. Game Play The opponent selects an unplayed piece. The player places the selected piece on an empty space. Game End The winner is the player who forms a line of four pieces that all share a characteristic. i.e. not the opponent who selected the final piece. e.g. all light. e.g. all short. Advanced variant A 2×2 square of four pieces that all share a characteristic also wins. [Rating: 1/10] It’s not too bad, I like all the sneaky ways to win. But also it’s too minimalist, nobody seems too attached to the results to play more.

[Rating: 2/10] In the long term, could be "solved"....not any time soon though.  The Good: For a limited number of plays you can outguess and out play your opponent in this abstract.  The Bad: Moves eventually become obvious and the game loses it's charm and playability.

[Rating: 2/10] A bit too calculable and dry for my tastes: the nice wooden components can't save me from the feeling that it's about computing all the possible next actions for your opponent in turn before taking the appropriate least-bad option. As someone who prefers to play more intuitively, I tend to feel I'm wasting (my and my opponent's) time when forced to play in this way but I don't see how the game could be approached differently.

[Rating: 2/10] It's 4 in a row! But you win when someone blunders! Yay, it's over! Played at mochalunt 2024

[Rating: 3/10] So, this game appears to be degenerately stalemate prone until the end game, and then it is simple computation.  The best you can do is notice when you can win and make sure you don't hand your opponent a piece that will make them win.  Opportunities to plan even one turn ahead appear to be exceedingly rare until you hit the point where you can plan out the rest of the game.  You can't even do basic forking strategies that emerge in most n-in-a-row games, since there is no ownership of pieces.
